newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's of London profits set to fall - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's of London profits set to fall - analyst.

text.p: Profits for Lloyds of London insurers are coming under pressure from lower rates, greater competiton and increased capacity, and will decline over the years 1994 to 1997, Syndicate Underwriting Research Limited (SURL) said.
SURL, which is a subsidiary of Anton Jardine Holdings Limited, projects percentage returns of 11.0 percent for 1994, 10.5 percent for 1995, six percent for 1996 and four percent for 1997.
Lloyd's reports results three years in arrears. Earlier this year, the insurance market announced a return to profit on 1993 after five years of record losses.

"The marine sector remains the most competitive for 1997. Non-marine continues to offer the best potential in 1996. Aviation is expected to perform below average. Motor is the first sector to show signs of recovery," SURL said in a statement.
The forecasts are bottom line returns and are stated before members' agent charges and levies on the 1994 and 1995 years.

Marine insurance has become a buyers' market, SURL said, with many insurers intent on maintaining premium volume. "From having the highest profit potential in 1993 and 1994 it is now forecast to have the lowest in 1997."
Marine rates are forecast to fall by 13 percent in 1996 and nine percent in 1997, bringing them below 1992 levels, it added.
Non-marine rates in 1997 will only be one percentage point above 1992 levels, SURL said.

"The absence of a very large catastrophe loss since Hurricane Andrew in 1992 has led to complacent underwriting standards worldwide, stronger balance sheets, a larger desire for market share and hence too much capacity."
SURL said it expects Lloyd's motor insurance syndicates would outperform their company rivals in 1995 and 1996 thanks to a greater exposure to non-standard risks, "quality of service and innovation".

Aviation has the second highest profit potential for 1996 of the four sectors. However, rating levels for 1996 are forecast to be 14 percentage points below 1995 with a further six point drop likely in 1997.

"The airline autumn renewals have seen a further softening in rates, and despite no shortage of well publicised airline disasters during 1996, it has been difficult to counter the demands of brokers and clients."
